summary: Specifies the initial configuration options of the Point-to-Point Protocol, as a Proposed Standard. These are the settings the two ends negotiate when setting up a link. It was replaced by RFC 1331 and RFC 1332.

plainLanguage.summary: Before two computers talk over a wire, they agree on settings. This lists the first settings they can agree on.

subtitle: The initial configuration options, link quality monitoring, and authentication methods for PPP.

tldr.problem: While RFC 1134 defined PPP itself, it didn't specify which configuration options systems should negotiate, how to monitor link quality, or how to authenticate peers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1172 defines seven Link Control Protocol options (maximum frame size, character mapping, authentication, magic numbers, quality monitoring, and two compression schemes), a Link Quality Report mechanism with counters, and the Password Authentication Protocol for simple credential exchange.
tldr.outcome: These initial options were later superseded by RFC 1331 (LCP options) and RFC 1332 (IPCP options), which separated and refined the specifications.

today: RFC 1331 superseded the LCP options, and RFC 1332 superseded the IPCP options, separating and refining the specifications.

sections.title: Configuration, Quality, and Authentication
sections.content:
RFC 1134 defined the Point-to-Point Protocol as a framework for transmitting datagrams over serial links. However, it left crucial details to future documents: which configuration parameters should the two ends negotiate? How can they verify that a link is actually working properly? How should one end confirm the other's identity?

RFC 1172 answers these questions by defining the initial set of configuration options that Link Control Protocol endpoints exchange, a Link Quality Monitoring mechanism for detecting and measuring packet loss, and the Password Authentication Protocol for peer authentication. These specifications allow PPP implementations to be interoperable while still permitting future extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers connecting over a modem need to agree on things like "How big can your packets be?" and "Are you who you say you are?" This document defines those first agreements.

sections.title: Link Control Protocol Configuration Options
sections.content:
The LCP allows both ends to negotiate modifications to the standard link. RFC 1172 defines seven initial option types.

Maximum-Receive-Unit (MRU) negotiates the largest frame each side can accept. The default is 1500 octets; endpoints can request smaller frames or advertise their ability to receive larger ones.

Async-Control-Character-Map (ACCM) is specific to asynchronous links. It's a 32-bit bitmap indicating which ASCII control characters must remain escaped. This lets systems negotiate which characters are safe to send unescaped through their particular serial hardware or modems.

Authentication-Type requests that the peer prove its identity using a specific authentication protocol before network data is exchanged. Multiple authentication protocols can be proposed; the implementation may accept one and reject the others. By default, no authentication is required.

Magic-Number is a random 32-bit value each endpoint chooses and transmits. If a system receives its own magic number echoed back, the link is looped-back (connected to itself). The magic number also aids in detecting misconfigured links connected to the wrong peer.

Link-Quality-Monitoring enables periodic link quality reports. The endpoint specifies a reporting period in microseconds; the peer sends Link-Quality-Report packets at that rate.

Protocol-Field-Compression allows compression of the PPP Protocol field from two octets to one, saving bandwidth on low-speed links. Compressed fields are only valid for data packets, never for LCP packets.

Address-and-Control-Field-Compression omits the constant Address (0xff) and Control (0x03) fields on non-ambiguous frames. This saves two bytes per packet but requires careful handling to prevent misinterpretation.
sections.plainLanguage: These are seven dials the computers turn: "How big are your packets?", "Which special characters do you need?", "Do you want to prove who you are?", "Here's my secret code to detect loops", "Tell me if the line is working", "Can I shorten some of my headers?"

sections.title: Monitoring Link Quality with LQR Packets
sections.content:
Real-world serial links drop packets, corrupt data, or lose synchronization. The Link Quality Monitoring (LQM) mechanism lets endpoints measure this loss without relying on upper-layer protocols.

LQM works by maintaining counters: each side counts the packets and octets it transmits and receives. Periodically (at the negotiated reporting period), each endpoint sends a Link-Quality-Report (LQR) packet to its peer. This packet contains the sender's transmission counters and the receiver's reception counters.

Upon receiving an LQR, the endpoint compares the reported received counts against what it actually transmitted in the previous period. If the counts don't match, packets or octets were lost. The endpoint calculates the packet loss percentage and can implement a link quality policy—a decision to accept the link, reroute traffic, or disconnect.

The beauty of LQM is that the mechanism (the LQR packet format and counters) is standardized, but the policy (what action to take on poor quality) is left to each implementation. One system might tolerate 5% loss; another might disconnect immediately. Both can interoperate as long as they understand the LQR format.

LQR packets have the highest transmission priority to ensure quality measurements remain accurate even when the link is congested. The LQR format includes three sections: a header (with code, identifier, and magic number), transmission counters from the sender, and reception counters that the receiver fills in.
sections.plainLanguage: Every few seconds, each side says "I sent 1000 packets, and you got 995 of them." By comparing these numbers, both sides know if the line is dropping too much data.

sections.title: The Password Authentication Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 1172 defines a simple Password Authentication Protocol (PAP) for optional authentication. When both sides agree via the Authentication-Type option to use PAP, an authentication phase begins after link quality testing but before network-layer protocol setup.

In PAP, the peer (the system that did not originate the connection) authenticates to the authenticator. The peer sends an Authenticate packet containing a user ID and a password in clear text. The authenticator responds with either an Authenticate-Ack (success) or Authenticate-Nak (failure), optionally including a message.

PAP is intentionally simple—it offers no encryption, and passwords travel in clear text. The RFC encourages the development of more secure authentication protocols. PAP is suitable only for environments where physical security or encryption at another layer protects the serial link.

The protocol is unidirectional: only one peer authenticates to the other. If both sides require authentication, they negotiate separate protocols in each direction. The implementation should allow configuration of which authentication protocols are acceptable, preventing attackers from negotiating weaker or no authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: PAP is the simplest password system: one side says "I'm Alice, my password is secret," and the other says "That's correct" or "Wrong.". It's not very secure, but it's simple.

sections.title: IP Control Protocol Options
sections.content:
The IP Control Protocol (IPCP) is the network-layer equivalent of LCP. While LCP configures the link itself, IPCP configures IP-specific parameters once LCP has established the connection.

IPCP uses the same packet format and state machine as LCP but negotiates IP-specific options. RFC 1172 defines two initial IPCP options: IP-Addresses and Compression-Type.

IP-Addresses allows both ends to negotiate their IP addresses. This is especially valuable on dial-up links where the client doesn't have a pre-assigned address. The initiator suggests both its own address and the peer's address; the peer can accept, suggest alternatives, or reject. This dynamic address assignment is crucial for large-scale dial-up systems.

Compression-Type enables header compression. Given that dial-up links often transfer interactive traffic (like Telnet) with small payloads and large headers, compressing the IP and TCP headers can significantly improve throughput. The option specifies which compression algorithm both sides will use.

IPCP negotiation cannot begin until LCP has completed the link quality phase. This ensures the physical link is stable before layer 3 setup. Only after successful IPCP negotiation can IP datagrams flow across the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the link is open, IPCP handles Internet-specific setup: "What IP address will you use?" and "Should we compress the headers?"
